Restart

Check the box to enable add-on debugging. Then click Load Temporary Add-On. Browse to your Firefox profile in appdata:

C:\Users<Username>\AppData\Roaming\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles<some random shit>.default\extensions

In the extensions folder there are .xpi files, those are your extensions that you had. Load each one and don't close Firefox until they fix this.

Agreed. Airbus came out with a totally redesigned airframe that competes directly with Boeing's 737 narrowbody class of passenger planes. Airbus's new frame and new engines combined allowed the plane to be operated at roughly 15% the cost as Boeing's, and at ~$3200 and hour, thats a lot of money over the year. So, what did Boeing do. Well instead of redesign their outdated airframe from the 60's, they figured they could get the newest, most efficient engines on the market and throw them on their aging airplanes wings and be done with it. In doing so, they realized that the new engines size and weight/thrust displacement ratios required the engines to be mounted further forward on the wing, and closer up to the underside of the wing. This caused some problems during flight at idle and above idle engine speeds; because the extra weight is shifted further forward on the wing, the air plane is naturally front heavy/bias, and relied on the engines to provide the thrust to keep the nose pointed slightly upward or else the plane would nose downward due to a loss of lift from the wings. Well, to counter act this Boeing's engineers decided to write some software that took this known issue into account for and allow it run in the background, SEPARATE of the FAA approved flight code. (All lines of flight coding has to be ran through the FAA line by line, top down, even if you change something from the very end. Very Expensive. And for laymen, FAA flight code was the base, and Boeing's software would come in "over the top" of the underlying code and "alter" the input numbers to satisfy and allow the FAA approved code to run properly without throwing error codes.) Well, this worked all fine and dandy, until they had a batch of bad Angle of Attack sensors (Small wings that stick out horizontal and perpendicular of the tube of the aircraft that measure the angle in which the air travels across the fuselage, by measuring the pitch angle of the sensor.) So, because some screws, or something rather wasn't holding these sensors together properly, the computer was getting bad information, and Boeing's bandaid of a software fix was sending fucked up information to the FAA certified autopilot computers which, apparently (and they haven't been very clear on this yet) was running in the background even WITH the autopilot turned OFF. Anyways, Boeing and the coding test division of the FAA is very likely going to be in some serious hot water soon because they had known about this "patch" and didn't include testing on the methods of it's operations.
